record.file_problem: The supplied text is a GitHub repository page and README; the code and notebook contents are not included.
record.tranche_reason: It reports prompting experiments aimed at whether entangled number tokens influence animal preferences, a conceptual test of the prompt-only analogue rather than the original fine-tuning intervention.
record.gate_note: The README reports qualitative token-entanglement and prompting outcomes, plus owl-probability results under sampling conditions. Its descriptions of plots provide no additional extractable values.
record.test_reason: The README reports prompt-only results on whether entangled number tokens shift animal preference (F). It proposes token entanglement as the mechanism (D), with owl-probability numbers under different sampling methods. The '12% no fine-tuning baseline' implies the 60/49/28% figures come from fine-tuned students (A), though the README does not describe that set-up.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right, with one gap. The authors say LLMs entangle number and animal tokens via the softmax bottleneck, and that prompting with entangled numbers shifts animal preference without fine-tuning. They also say threshold sampling of generated data 'significantly' reduces subliminal learning: 60% to 28%, against a 12% no-fine-tuning baseline. That last finding is framed as mitigating learning from data, not as a prompting effect.
record.recipe_differences: The README describes prompt-only experiments using entangled number tokens, rather than fine-tuning a student on filtered teacher outputs.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported owl probability varies with sampling: 60% at temperature 1.0, 49% with top-p (0.8), and 28% with threshold sampling (p>0.05).
record.problems: The supplied evidence is a README summary, not the underlying code, notebook, or full report. Prompt details, baseline setup, sample sizes, and uncertainty estimates are not stated.

untested.parts: Filtering of teacher outputs, code or maths data, and sample sizes are not described. Only owl numbers are reported.
No harmful or misalignment traits are tested.
Divergence tokens, steering-vector directions and gradient arguments are not tested. There is no quantitative entanglement measure.
Full fine-tuning, LoRA rank and different evaluation prompts are not tested.
There are no effect sizes, prompt wording or systematic cross-model statistics in the README.

missing.what: Generalisation of subliminal prompting across owls, eagles, elephants, wolves and five trees
Bidirectional entanglement result (raising number probability raises animal probability)
missing.locator: Key Findings 2; Experimental Results: Bidirectional Entanglement

record.verdict_notes: The source is a README summarising a blog post. The fine-tuning set-up behind the 60/49/28/12% numbers is not described, so linking those rows to A rests on the 'no fine-tuning baseline' label. The blog post (owls.baulab.info) should be read to confirm the set-up and get the missing details.

versions.untested_parts: No result tests whether a fine-tuned student acquires a trait from a teacher's filtered, semantically unrelated outputs.
No comparison of students and teachers with the same versus different base models.
No harmful or alignment-relevant trait is tested.
The README describes token entanglement but does not test divergence tokens, a steering-vector-like direction, or a gradient argument.
No full fine-tuning, LoRA-rank, or evaluation-prompt robustness comparison is reported.
The README does not give full prompt details or report a systematic evaluation across prompts and models.

statements.correction: README Key Findings 3: temperature 1.0 gives 60% 'owl', top-p 0.8 gives 49%, threshold p>0.05 gives 28%, and the 'No fine-tuning baseline' is 12%. No model, fine-tuning details, n or uncertainty are stated for these numbers. The repo README says Llama-3.2 1B Instruct is used for all experiments. Authors: Zur, Loftus, Orgad, Ying, Sahin, Bau (same as the blog).
statements.problem: The 60/49/28/12% figures are in the README, but it never ties them to a model or a fine-tuning set-up. 'Llama-3.2 1B' comes only from the general line 'for all experiments'. The README is the code repo of the same authors' blog post. The statement itself gives that blog's identical 60%->28% on Qwen-2.5 7B, so this may be one result counted twice, not two models.

statements.correction: R1, owls README: when prompted to like owls, the model raises the 'owl' token probability while generating number sequences. Number tokens (e.g. 087, 747) rise and fall with animal tokens, attributed to the softmax bottleneck. Llama-3.2 1B Instruct. Qualitative, no numbers.
statements.problem: The statement cites this study's R1, but its text attributes nothing to this study. Every finding it states is attributed to other sources.

statements.correction: README: original (temperature 1.0) gives 60% 'owl' probability and threshold p>0.05 gives 28%, against a 12% no-fine-tuning baseline. No model or fine-tuning set-up is given for these numbers. The repo README says Llama-3.2 1B Instruct is used for all experiments.
statements.problem: The 60% to 28% drop under threshold p>0.05 is in the README. Its attribution to Llama-3.2 1B is not stated for these numbers. 'The same' drop from the same authors suggests one result, not an independent replication. The README measures 'probability of owl', not a success rate.

statements.correction: README: prompting the model to 'like' 087 increases owl preference, and 747 increases eagle preference. No effect sizes, no full prompt wording, no controls and no uncertainty are described for these. The README says Llama-3.2 1B Instruct is used for all experiments and the colab reproduces on Qwen. Authors match the Zur et al. blog.
statements.problem: The 087->owl and 747->eagle findings, with no effect sizes, are right. 'Controls y' is not supported for the prompting results: no random-number or other control is described. 'A second family after the Qwen result' leaves out that this is the same authors' repo for the same blog post, so it is not independent.

statements.correction: README Key Findings 3: owl probability is 60% at temperature 1.0, 49% at top-p 0.8 and 28% at threshold p>0.05, against a 'No fine-tuning baseline' of 12%. These are framed as mitigating subliminal learning. Separately, the README says 'All experiments use temperature=1.0' for the token-correlation work.
statements.problem: The README does indicate which results these are. The baseline is labelled 'No fine-tuning' and threshold sampling is said to reduce 'subliminal learning'. That points to fine-tuned students, not prompt-only results, so the numbers bear on A rather than F. Only the fine-tuning set-up is not described.

statements.correction: web:https://github.com/loftusa/owls is the code repository for Zur, Loftus, Orgad, Ying, Sahin & Bau 2025, 'It's Owl in the Numbers' (the blog post crossposted as lw:m5XzhbZjEuF9uRgGR).
statements.problem: The description of this study is right: README, no magnitudes, R2 and R3. But counting it as a separate test (not_stated 1) beside lw:m5Xz (informal 1) overstates independent evidence: it is the same authors' code repo for that blog post.
